crime.value: Murder of a child victim (implied); central question: how did the detective manipulate evidence and exploit the crime scene to frame an innocent man (Sonny Mossman) for execution?
crime.quote: He pulled on his gloves and looked around...He then selected a hair bow from a drawer...slipped inside his jacket pocket.

victim.value: A young girl, murdered by an unknown assailant; her body was placed in Sonny Mossman's car trunk, making her 'killable' because her death provided the detective opportunity for corruption.
victim.quote: fed a guy who had a little girl locked up in the trunk of his car

closed_world.value: The penitentiary Death Tank (execution chamber) and the diner where the final meal is prepared; a system bounded by state authority, judicial finality, and the irreversibility of capital punishment.
closed_world.quote: The Restraint Team ran the Death Tank because some cons lose it at the end...Sonny Mossman looked up from where he sat on the slab bed

culprit_and_motive.value: The detective; motive is to execute Sonny Mossman by framing him with planted evidence (fabricated fingerprint and hair from victim's room), possibly to close a case, hide his own knowledge, or enact vigilante justice.
culprit_and_motive.quote: Using a prepared strip of tape, he lifted one perfect print...He slipped them into a manila coin envelope...He made the case.

resolution.value: Incomplete/ambiguous. The detective's manipulation succeeds mechanically—Mossman is executed ('two thousand volts')—but no official exposure or justice occurs. The resolution is the execution itself, restoring institutional order while concealing systemic corruption.
resolution.quote: Two thousand volts. Sam rolled over and hoped his appetite would return in the morning.

investigator.value: Sam, the diner grill man; he serves as witness and moral mirror. He suspects the detective's corruption but cannot act. The reader experiences the mystery through his dawning awareness and complicity.
investigator.quote: Sam felt weird about the detective...Did the detective blame Sam for having served somebody he didn't know was a killer?

suspect_architecture.value: Minimal cast: convicted killer Sonny Mossman (the condemned, no active suspense role), unnamed detective (investigator-turned-schemer), Cooper (prison employee/delivery man, unwitting accomplice), Sam (grill man, passive witness). Mossman is the established guilty party for a child murder; the detective is the morally ambiguous actor planting evidence. No competing suspects — architecture is inverted, focused on justice-outside-law rather than whodunit.
suspect_architecture.quote: He had just found Mossman's abandoned car in the woods. Nobody else knew yet.

red_herring.value: The thumping sound Cooper hears from the trunk briefly evokes the possibility of a living victim inside — mirroring Mossman's own crime of transporting a girl in a trunk — but it is merely the food sack tipping over. This false trail momentarily implicates Cooper in something sinister and echoes the original crime.
red_herring.quote: he thought he heard a thumping inside the trunk. It stopped his heart for a second.

clue_fairness.value: The reader is shown every element of the scheme in real time: the detective watching which burger goes into the bag, Sam stuffing napkins into the sack, Mossman finding a used napkin with writing on it, and the detective's flashback to lifting a print and collecting hair from the girl's room. All physical evidence of the planted message and framing materials is presented to the reader before Mossman encounters them.
clue_fairness.quote: He saw the wet wrinkle first and realized that this was a used napkin... unfolding the napkin further, he saw the writing.

social_world.value: Layered institutional hierarchy: the prison system (Restraint Team, Cooper as low-rung employee trading night shifts for tuition reimbursement, unnamed bosses issuing orders), the detective as lone moral agent outside that hierarchy, death-row protesters as powerless idealists, and Sam as working-class everyman caught between them. Power flows from the state downward; the detective exploits gaps in the chain of command.
social_world.quote: He worked at the pen because it was a night job and they reimbursed half his tuition... He did what he was told.

alibi.value: The detective constructs a retrospective alibi of legitimacy by having planted genuine physical evidence (a fingerprint lifted from the girl's china tea set, two strands of her hair) — evidence that will appear to confirm Mossman's guilt through proper forensic channels, obscuring that it was planted. The 'alibi' here is institutional: the evidence will speak for itself, placing the detective above suspicion.
alibi.quote: Using a prepared strip of tape, he lifted one perfect print... He then selected a hair bow... He made the case. He did his job.

reveal_mechanic.value: The reveal is tactile and material: Mossman recognises the handwriting on the napkin from court papers — the name of his victim written in a hand he knows. The mechanism is handwriting identification, delivered through the intimacy of a last meal ritual, converting a mundane object (a napkin) into a devastating psychological confrontation.
reveal_mechanic.quote: He recognized the penmanship right off. He knew it from the court papers. Sonny read the girl's name, and then his eyes lost focus.

media_and_audience.value: The execution is a public spectacle framed by death-penalty protesters outside the prison gates with signs, bullhorns, and candles. Their presence packages the crime as a cause rather than a case, and the narrative ironises their moral certainty. The power grid flicker is registered across the county as a 'complicit blink,' making the execution a shared, ambient media event experienced even by Sam in the diner.
media_and_audience.quote: Sam imagined an aerial view, lights dimming all across the county in one long, complicit blink.

investigator_wound.value: The detective's wound is dual: a terminal prostate cancer diagnosis that converted him to vegetarianism and forced three years of abstinence from red meat, now broken to carry out this act — his body literally suffering for his moral transgression. More deeply, he cannot let the case rest on legitimate evidence alone, suggesting a wound of institutional distrust or a personal bond to the murdered girl that compels him to guarantee the outcome himself.
investigator_wound.quote: Prostate cancer had turned him into a vegetarian... Three-plus years without red meat, until today. The meal burned like a cancer in his belly.
